rewritten_text:
Do you come back often?"

"I haven't been here since."

"Neither have I."

The moon began rising, and I remembered the peaceful look directed at the white ceiling, a look that was gone forever. The moon began rising, and I remembered the pressure of his hand on mine as I spoke the last words he would hear in this life.

After a silence, Estella spoke again.

"I've often wanted and planned to return, but so many things prevented it. Poor, poor old place!"

The first moonlight touched the silvery mist and the tears falling from her eyes. She did not realize I could see them. Trying to control herself, she said quietly,

"Were you wondering as you walked here why the place had been left in this condition?"

"Yes, Estella."

"I own the land. It's the only thing I haven't given up. Everything else has gone, bit by bit, but I kept this. Holding on to it was the only firm stand I made through all those miserable years."

"Are they going to build on it?"

"Yes, finally. I've come to say goodbye before it changes. And you," she said with a concern that moved me, a man so often away from home, "do you still live abroad?"

"Yes."

"And you're doing well, I'm sure?"

"I work quite hard and earn enough to live on. So yes, I'm doing well."

"I've thought about you often," Estella said.

"Have you?"

"Very often lately. For a long, difficult time I refused to remember what I had thrown away without knowing its worth. But since remembering no longer goes against my duty, I've let that memory into my heart."

"You have always had your place in mine," I replied.

We fell silent again until she spoke.

"I never expected," Estella said, "that saying goodbye to this place would also mean saying goodbye to you. I'm very glad of the chance."

"Glad to part again, Estella? Saying goodbye hurts me. Remembering our last parting has always brought me sadness and pain."

"But you said to me," she answered earnestly, "'God bless you, God forgive you!' If you could say that then, you won't hesitate to say it now. Suffering has taught me more than anything else ever could. It has helped me understand what you used to feel. I've been bent and broken, but I hope the result is something better.

With everything settled so pleasantly and satisfactorily, they solemnly sealed their agreement over another teacup of the peppermint mixture. The lady's excitement and nervousness made this seem all the more necessary. While they drank, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

"Very well," he said, sipping his peppermint. "I'll stop at Sowerberry's on my way home and tell him to send someone tomorrow morning. Was that what frightened you, my love?"

"Nothing in particular, dear," the lady replied, avoiding the question.

"It must have been something, love," Mr. Bumble insisted. "Won't you tell your own B.?"

"Not now," she answered. "Someday. After we're married, dear."

"After we're married!" Mr. Bumble exclaimed. "It wasn't any cheek from one of those male paupers that—"

"No, no, love!" she quickly interrupted.

"If I thought it was," Mr. Bumble continued, "if I thought one of them dared raise his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—"

"They wouldn't dare, love," the lady assured him.

"They'd better not!" Mr. Bumble said, clenching his fist. "Let me catch any man, from this parish or anywhere else, trying it. I guarantee he wouldn't do it a second time!"

Without the violent gestures, this might not have sounded like much praise for the lady's beauty. But Mr. Bumble accompanied his threat with so many warlike movements that she was deeply touched by his devotion. Admiringly, she declared that he truly was a dove.

The dove turned up his coat collar and put on his three-cornered hat. After sharing a long, loving embrace with his future wife, he went out once more into the cold night wind. He paused only a few minutes in the male paupers' ward to abuse its occupants a little. This reassured him that he could perform the workhouse master's duties with the necessary harshness. Satisfied with his abilities, he left cheerfully, imagining his future promotion all the way to the undertaker's shop.

Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper. Noah Claypole, meanwhile, never cared to exert himself beyond what was needed to eat and drink comfortably. Consequently, the shop remained open well after its usual closing time. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane against the counter several times without attracting anyone's attention. Seeing light through the glass window of the little back parlour, he ventured to look in and discover what was happening. The sight gave him quite a surprise.

There was plenty of cold water to finish their meal. After a while, Becky suggested they start moving again. Tom hesitated, then spoke.

"Becky, can you handle something I need to tell you?"

Her face went pale, but she thought she could.

"Then, Becky, we have to stay here where there's drinking water. That little stub is our last candle."

Becky began sobbing and crying out. Tom tried everything he could to comfort her, with little success. Finally she said,

"Tom!"

"Yes, Becky?"

"They'll notice we're missing and come looking!"

"Yes, they will! Of course they will!"

"Maybe they're already searching, Tom."

"Maybe they are. I hope so."

"When would they notice we're gone?"

"When they get back to the boat, I suppose."

"But it might be dark then, Tom. Would they realize we hadn't come?"

"I don't know. Anyway, your mother would notice as soon as everyone got home."

The frightened expression on Becky's face made Tom realize his mistake. She wasn't supposed to go home that night. Both children fell silent, thinking. A moment later Becky burst into fresh tears, showing him that she had reached the same conclusion: Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher learned that Becky wasn't at Mrs. Harper's.

They stared at their scrap of candle as it melted slowly and mercilessly away. At last only half an inch of wick remained. They watched the weak flame rise and sink, climb the thin thread of smoke, hover briefly at its tip, and vanish. The horror of complete darkness took over.

Neither child could say how much time passed before Becky gradually became aware that she was crying in Tom's arms. They knew only that, after what seemed an immense stretch of time, they both woke from a heavy, exhausted sleep and returned to their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday by then, perhaps even Monday. He tried to draw Becky into conversation, but grief overwhelmed her and she had lost all hope. He assured her that they must have been missed long ago and that people were surely searching. He would shout; perhaps someone would come. He tried, but the distant echoes sounded so dreadful in the darkness that he did not try again.

The hours slipped away, and hunger returned to torment the prisoners. A piece remained of Tom's half of the cake. They divided it and ate, but afterward they felt hungrier than ever.
